detail: Within 5% of the high counts as close to the top, and the S&P 500 closed at 7,592.40 on Thursday, about 2.9% below its record close of 7,818.93 on 6 October. It slipped only 0.35% as Nvidia's chief executive resigned, a small move given the news.
source: CNBC closing figures via The Company Chronicle, 12 Nov; record close from Anadolu and EdgeX, 6 Oct

detail: Breadth was narrow on Thursday: on the Nasdaq, new 52-week lows outnumbered new highs by 266, and in the S&P 500 about three shares fell for every one that rose. When most shares fall while the index only dips, the selling is wider than the headline suggests.
source: TheStreet Pro (Nasdaq new highs minus new lows) and Dean Financials (S&P 500 advancers and decliners), 12 Nov

detail: Above 4.5% counts as high, and the US 10-year yield closed at 5.10% on Thursday, up from 4.98% on Tuesday, as bond markets reopened after the holiday and priced in more Fed rate rises. Safe government bonds paying over 5% set a high bar for shares to beat.
source: US Treasury daily yield curve via The Company Chronicle, 12 Nov

detail: Markets expect rates to go up: fed funds futures were pricing three quarter-point Fed rises by March, starting on 9 December, and economists at ING expect another Bank of England rise by February, with December also seen as possible. Higher rates make borrowing dearer and tend to weigh on share prices, especially fast-growing companies.
source: CME FedWatch via CNBC, 12 Nov; ING via MT Newswires and CNBC on the Bank of England, 12 Nov

detail: Above $90 a barrel counts as expensive, and Brent crude settled at $95.82 on Thursday, up 3.3%, after President Trump said the US doesn't need a deal with Iran. Dear oil keeps pressure on inflation, which is one reason central banks are raising rates.
